name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q01 - Preparation steps of potassium dichromate from chromite

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps involved in the industrial preparation of potassium dichromate (\(\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}\)) from chromite ore (\(\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4}\)) in the correct chronological sequence:

  • Acidification of yellow sodium chromate solution with sulphuric acid to obtain orange sodium dichromate.
  • Fusion of chromite ore with sodium carbonate in free access of air to form sodium chromate.
  • Treatment of sodium dichromate solution with potassium chloride to crystallise orange potassium dichromate.
  • Filtration of the yellow sodium chromate solution to remove insoluble iron(III) oxide.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Potassium dichromate is prepared from chromite ore (\(\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4}\)) through oxidative alkaline fusion to form chromate, followed by separation of insoluble impurities, conversion of chromate to dichromate in acidic medium, and double decomposition with potassium chloride.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Stage
First, chromite ore is fused with sodium carbonate in free access of air to produce yellow sodium chromate and insoluble iron(III) oxide:
\(4\mathrm{FeCr_2O_4} + 8\mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 7\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 8\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3} + 8\mathrm{CO_2}\).
Second, the yellow solution of sodium chromate is filtered to remove the insoluble \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\).
Third, the filtered sodium chromate solution is acidified with sulphuric acid to form sodium dichromate:
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\).
Fourth, because potassium dichromate is less soluble than sodium dichromate, treating the sodium dichromate solution with potassium chloride precipitates orange crystals of potassium dichromate:
\(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{KCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence is: Fusion of chromite ore with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in air \(\rightarrow\) Filtration of yellow \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\) solution \(\rightarrow\) Acidification with \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Treatment with \(\mathrm{KCl}\).

answer.text: Filtration of \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\) solution \(\rightarrow\) Fusion of chromite ore with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in air \(\rightarrow\) Acidification with \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Treatment with \(\mathrm{KCl}\)

Fusion of chromite ore with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in air \(\rightarrow\) Acidification with \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Filtration of \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\) solution \(\rightarrow\) Treatment with \(\mathrm{KCl}\)

Fusion of chromite ore with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in air \(\rightarrow\) Filtration of \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\) solution \(\rightarrow\) Acidification with \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Treatment with \(\mathrm{KCl}\)

Fusion of chromite ore with \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\) in air \(\rightarrow\) Treatment with \(\mathrm{KCl}\) \(\rightarrow\) Filtration of \(\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4}\) solution \(\rightarrow\) Acidification with \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q02 - Commercial preparation steps of potassium permanganate

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following stages in the commercial preparation of potassium permanganate (\(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\)) from pyrolusite ore (\(\mathrm{MnO_2}\)) in the correct sequential order:

  • Electrolytic oxidation of manganate(VI) ion in alkaline solution
  • Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) with \(\mathrm{KOH}\) and an oxidising agent
  • Formation of purple permanganate ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\))
  • Formation of dark green potassium manganate (\(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Commercial synthesis of potassium permanganate proceeds in two main chemical steps: first, oxidation of manganese(IV) oxide to manganese(VI) in molten alkali, and second, electrolytic oxidation of manganese(VI) to manganese(VII).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Stage
Initially, pyrolusite ore (\(\mathrm{MnO_2}\)) undergoes alkaline oxidative fusion with \(\mathrm{KOH}\) in the presence of air or \(\mathrm{KNO_3}\):
\(2\mathrm{MnO_2} + 4\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\).
This reaction yields dark green potassium manganate (\(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\)) containing the \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\) ion.
Subsequently, the manganate(VI) ion is subjected to electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution, which converts it into the purple permanganate ion (\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is: Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Formation of dark green \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution \(\rightarrow\) Formation of purple \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\).

answer.text: Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Formation of dark green \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution \(\rightarrow\) Formation of purple \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)

Electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution \(\rightarrow\) Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Formation of dark green \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Formation of purple \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)

Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution \(\rightarrow\) Formation of purple \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) \(\rightarrow\) Formation of dark green \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\)

Formation of dark green \(\mathrm{K_2MnO_4}\) \(\rightarrow\) Electrolytic oxidation in alkaline solution \(\rightarrow\) Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) \(\rightarrow\) Formation of purple \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q03 - Increasing spin only magnetic moment of divalent ions

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following aqueous divalent ions of the \(3d\) transition series in the increasing order of their calculated spin-only magnetic moments:

\(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 25\)), \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 28\)), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 26\)), \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 29\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are given four aqueous divalent \(3d\) transition metal ions: \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 25\)), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 26\)), \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 28\)), and \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 29\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Relevant Formulae
For first-row transition metal ions, the orbital angular momentum contribution is quenched, so the magnetic moment is given by the spin-only formula:
\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\mathrm{BM}\), where \(n\) is the number of unpaired electrons. When forming \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ions, the \(4s\) electrons are lost first.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
1. \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 29\)): Ground state is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^1\), so \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) has \(3d^9\) configuration with \(n = 1\) unpaired electron.
\(\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\,\mathrm{BM}\).
2. \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 28\)): Ground state is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^84s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) has \(3d^8\) configuration with \(n = 2\) unpaired electrons.
\(\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.84\,\mathrm{BM}\).
3. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 26\)): Ground state is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^64s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) has \(3d^6\) configuration with \(n = 4\) unpaired electrons.
\(\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\,\mathrm{BM}\).
4. \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (\(Z = 25\)): Ground state is \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^54s^2\), so \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) has \(3d^5\) configuration with \(n = 5\) unpaired electrons.
\(\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\,\mathrm{BM}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since \(1.73 < 2.84 < 4.90 < 5.92\), the increasing order of spin-only magnetic moments is \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} < \mathrm{Ni^{2+}} < \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} < \mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q04 - Increasing oxidising power of transition metal oxospecies

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following oxo-species of first-row transition metals in the increasing order of their oxidising power in acidic medium:

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\), \(\mathrm{VO_2^+}\), \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In acidic aqueous solution, the oxidising power of high-oxidation-state oxo-species increases with the increasing stability of the lower oxidation state species to which they are reduced.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Species
1. \(\mathrm{VO_2^+}\) contains vanadium in the \(+5\) oxidation state, which is reduced to \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\) or \(\mathrm{V^{3+}}\).
2. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\) contains chromium in the \(+6\) oxidation state, which is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) (\(E^\circ = 1.33\,\mathrm{V}\)).
3. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) contains manganese in the \(+7\) oxidation state, which is reduced to the particularly stable half-filled \(3d^5\) \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ion (\(E^\circ = 1.52\,\mathrm{V}\)).
As the stability of the reduced lower-oxidation-state species increases from vanadium to chromium to manganese, the tendency of the parent oxo-species to accept electrons increases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, the increasing order of oxidising power is \(\mathrm{VO_2^+} < \mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} < \mathrm{MnO_4^-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q05 - Decreasing order of melting points of 3d metals

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following \(3d\) transition metals in the decreasing order of their melting points:

\(\mathrm{Cr}\), \(\mathrm{Mn}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}\), \(\mathrm{V}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The high melting points of transition metals are attributed to strong interatomic metallic bonding involving both \(ns\) and unpaired \((n-1)d\) electrons. In any transition series, melting points generally rise to a maximum at the \(d^5\) configuration, except for an anomalous dip at manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\)) and technetium (\(\mathrm{Tc}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Metal
1. Chromium (\(\mathrm{Cr}\), \(3d^54s^1\)) has the maximum number of unpaired electrons (six unpaired electrons) available for interatomic metallic bonding, giving it the highest melting point in the \(3d\) series.
2. Vanadium (\(\mathrm{V}\), \(3d^34s^2\)) has strong metallic bonding with three \(3d\) electrons and ranks below chromium.
3. Iron (\(\mathrm{Fe}\), \(3d^64s^2\)) has four unpaired \(3d\) electrons after pairing begins, giving it a lower melting point than vanadium.
4. Manganese (\(\mathrm{Mn}\), \(3d^54s^2\)), despite having five \(3d\) electrons, exhibits an anomalously low melting point (lower than \(\mathrm{Fe}\) and \(\mathrm{V}\)) due to the stability of its half-filled \(3d^5\) configuration, which makes its \(d\) electrons less available for metallic bonding.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, the decreasing order of melting points is \(\mathrm{Cr} > \mathrm{V} > \mathrm{Fe} > \mathrm{Mn}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q06 - Increasing ionic radii of trivalent lanthanoid ions

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following trivalent lanthanoid ions in the increasing order of their ionic radii:

\(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 57\)), \(\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 64\)), \(\mathrm{Yb^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 70\)), \(\mathrm{Nd^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 60\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Across the lanthanoid series from lanthanum (\(Z = 57\)) to lutetium (\(Z = 71\)), there is a regular decrease in the ionic radii of \(\mathrm{Ln^{3+}}\) ions with increasing atomic number. This phenomenon is known as lanthanoid contraction and is caused by the imperfect shielding of one \(4f\) electron by another in the same subshell as the nuclear charge increases.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Ion
Ordering the given ions by decreasing atomic number (from smallest radius to largest radius):
1. \(\mathrm{Yb^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 70\)) has the highest nuclear charge among the four and therefore the smallest ionic radius (\(86\,\mathrm{pm}\)).
2. \(\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 64\)) has a larger radius (\(94\,\mathrm{pm}\)) than \(\mathrm{Yb^{3+}}\).
3. \(\mathrm{Nd^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 60\)) has a larger radius (\(99\,\mathrm{pm}\)) than \(\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}\).
4. \(\mathrm{La^{3+}}\) (\(Z = 57\)) has the lowest nuclear charge among the four and therefore the largest ionic radius (\(106\,\mathrm{pm}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of ionic radii is \(\mathrm{Yb^{3+}} < \mathrm{Gd^{3+}} < \mathrm{Nd^{3+}} < \mathrm{La^{3+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q07 - Increasing standard reduction potentials of M3+ to M2+ couples

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following redox couples of first-row transition elements in the increasing order of their standard electrode potential \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{3+}/M^{2+}})\) values:

\(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}/Co^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard reduction potential \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{3+}/M^{2+}})\) measures the tendency of \(\mathrm{M^{3+}}\) to be reduced to \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) in aqueous solution, which depends on the third ionisation enthalpy, electronic configuration stability (\(d^3\), \(d^5\)), and hydration enthalpy.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Redox Couple
1. \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}}\) has a negative \(E^\circ\) value (\(-0.41\,\mathrm{V}\)) because \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) (\(d^3\), half-filled \(t_{2g}\) level) is much more stable in aqueous solution than \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) (\(d^4\)).
2. \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}\) has a moderately positive \(E^\circ\) value (\(+0.77\,\mathrm{V}\)) because \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\) possesses the extra-stable half-filled \(d^5\) configuration.
3. \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}}\) has a high positive \(E^\circ\) value (\(+1.57\,\mathrm{V}\)) because reduction converts \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) (\(d^4\)) into the very stable half-filled \(d^5\) \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) ion.
4. \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}/Co^{2+}}\) has the highest positive \(E^\circ\) value among these (\(+1.97\,\mathrm{V}\)), making \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) an exceptionally strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Comparing the values (\(-0.41\,\mathrm{V} < +0.77\,\mathrm{V} < +1.57\,\mathrm{V} < +1.97\,\mathrm{V}\)), the increasing order is \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr^{2+}} < \mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} < \mathrm{Mn^{3+}/Mn^{2+}} < \mathrm{Co^{3+}/Co^{2+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_UNIT8_Q08 - Increasing basic character of vanadium oxides

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following oxides of vanadium in the increasing order of their basic character:

\(\mathrm{V_2O_3}\), \(\mathrm{V_2O_5}\), \(\mathrm{V_2O_4}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For transition metal oxides, as the oxidation state of the metal increases, the ionic character decreases and the covalent and acidic character increases. Consequently, lower oxides are basic while higher oxides are amphoteric or acidic.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Oxide
1. In \(\mathrm{V_2O_5}\), vanadium is in its highest oxidation state (\(+5\)); it is amphoteric though mainly acidic, reacting with alkalies as well as acids.
2. In \(\mathrm{V_2O_4}\), vanadium is in the \(+4\) oxidation state; it is less basic than \(\mathrm{V_2O_3}\) and dissolves in acids to give \(\mathrm{VO^{2+}}\) salts.
3. In \(\mathrm{V_2O_3}\), vanadium is in the \(+3\) oxidation state; having the lowest oxidation number among the three, it has the highest ionic character and is distinctly basic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Since basic character decreases as the oxidation state of vanadium increases from \(+3\) to \(+5\), the increasing order of basic character is \(\mathrm{V_2O_5} < \mathrm{V_2O_4} < \mathrm{V_2O_3}\).
